First Hitchcock miss. Some cool ideas, sure, and great cinematographic technique at play here, but this was just a poor plot in my opinion. Starts off quite good, loses momentum halfway through completely and never gets it back. An impactful ending is attempted but seems cheap to me. I was disappointed by Jimmy Stewart here, I still think he’s an incredible actor but this wasn’t great. Kim Novak was good though.
Beautifully shot and an incredible score, especially for its time, but I just can’t get behind Stewart’s performance and the twist is a little uninspiring.

The first thing I liked that Hitchcock did was add a point of view to the film. When watching and seeing from Scottie's point of view, it helps you have a better understanding of the movie. We see this constantly when Scottie is driving and is following Madeline through San Francisco. From this, you can see Scottie, but you also get to see where he is going and how he is constantly following her. The point-of-view shot was used multiple times in the film, and another time is when he is running up the stairs at the church trying to save Madeline. In this scene, the point-of-view shot shows Scottie's acrophobia and how it is preventing him from saving the love of his life. To add on, in this scene, the dolly zoom was used to emphasize his fear and add suspense to the film to see if he will be able to save her. The dolly zoom was used twice, and both times it was to show his fear. In my opinion, the first dolly zoom was foreshadowing because his fear led to someone dying, and then later in the film that happened again when he was running up the church; even though fake Madeline didn’t die, Scottie thought she did. I also think that color in this film was very important and adds to Scottie's obsession because when we see Scottie, there is usually something red around him; for example, we once saw Scottie wearing a red suit, and red reflects danger and evil, and at the end of the movie Scotties obssesion caused him to become evil towards judy especaillywhen he made her wear the certian clothes. In my opinion, the “Cardinal Sins of Cinema” I struggled with the most in this movie was it being too slow. It's weird because there were times when I felt that some scenes were too long and some were too short. Times when I thought it was too long were when Scottie was driving and following Madeline, for example when they were driving into the woods and the bay; I felt that they could have been just a little shorter. I also wish that the ending scene was longer because I feel that the ending was abrupt. She fell through the window, then it just ended. In my opinion, I prefer when movie endings wrap up the story more and not leave it up for interpretation. Some people may think this movie is too old, but I honestly don't think so because I know if I had watched this in 1958, I would have been gagged by the plot twist. The coloring of this film also adds another element to it that makes it a classic. I feel like I didn’t enjoy it as much because I am used to watching movies now with better action and more complex plot twists. Overall, though, I feel this still can be considered a movie classic even though I would never rewatch it again.

Vertigo interests me as a foundation for the future of films. While I did enjoy it, I consider this film GOOD, but not GREAT. It's narrative is interesting, and honestly clearly well thought out, but not perfectly executed. I loved the reveal of the mystery, but hated how it was revealed to the audience, while still having an hour of the film left. I like the theory that Scottie has ling before figured it out, and is testing Judy, but so little evidemce is given to support that, that i'm not sure if i'm just reaching. Hitchcock makes very bold creative decisions, especially for 1958 under classic cinemas systems. I love how he blends animation with live action footage for the nightmare sequence, adding psychedelic imagery to an audience who obviously hated it, as well as LOVING his use of colour on set and costume to subtly showcase themes of greed, love, and obsession to the point of destruction. It's really fun to look back on certain moments with that in mind. However the negatives really out weigh my opinion of the film, like how Scottie's vertigo really is underused, and the ending of this film is genuinely the worst film ending I've ever seen, it felt like they got to the end of the script snd just said fuck it, idk what to do 😭. Hitchcock's vision, and directing is impressive, but not that well excecuted. Overall with all the hype I expected A LOT better of a film. But still interesting to see a foundation for Hollywoods later creatives to have surely taking inspiration from! But it did give us the Dolly Zoom, so that's pretty cool! :) (Also random note, I can't help but feel like Tim Burtons Batman is heavily inspired by this film lmaooo)

I was very shocked by the way the film ended because I was not expecting the story to take the direction that it did. After Madeleine supposedly committed suicide, John became obsessed with her and was unable to move on. When Judy came into his life, he wanted to change everything about her so that she would resemble Madeleine. Eventually, John took Judy back to the bell tower where Madeleine had “died” , the reason why he took Judy there was because he wanted to relive what had happened and become the hero he was not able to be the first time. Judy was scared and upset about being there, but John was determined to make it to the top. Once they reached the top of the bell tower, Judy became startled when she saw a shadowy figure and backed away and ended up falling to her death. I think the way that this movie was created was beautiful. There were a lot of colors, lighting, and sound effects that really stood out to me. For instance, when Judy is done with her makeover to look like Madeleine, there is a part where she steps out of the powder room and the lighting changes. Judy looks sad at first, but then she starts to smile, while John looks at her almost like he is seeing the ghost of Madeleine. This scene stuck with me because the expressions of the characters, lighting, and the sound effects, make everything seem eerie and unsettling. I think that this film is important to film studies because of the cinematography, along with the psychological effects that it produces. For instance, the obsession that John has with trying to make Judy more like Madeleine is quite alarming and can make for an interesting topic in studies.

Coming out of Rear Window , my expectations for Hitchcock were that this would be a small, yet creatively-shot movie. Instead, it was massive, intricate, and impressive from all filmmaking standpoints—until its throwaway of an ending. Vertigo was a dark and complex story which keeps its audience on edge and guessing as there is never a moment where at least one of its characters isn’t going insane. It’s not a simple story with simple characters like Rear Window , and it definitely doesn’t leave anyone with a good feeling. The tricks that Hitchcock used to make some of the sequences magnificent are incredible to learn about, and the visuals—whether they be the stunning, colorfully-charged cinematography or the masterworks of 1950s editing that makes us feel uncomfortable yet fill us with wonder at the same time, this is a journey. The pure intention behind the focuses and the frames and even the shapes leave the viewer with a lot to dissect, until the ending discourages everything. This film was written incredibly well and its plot twist was a genuine shock. It felt like, through all its twists and turns, it was building up to a magnificent crescendo, but instead, its ending seemed to forget everything about the movie. Sure, it may seem like poetic justice, but that doesn’t change the fact that it didn’t make sense. Hitchcock impressed me with Vertigo, but I left frustrated as all the bells and whistles and hooks didn’t pay off in the end. For a journey of all sorts that never finds its destination, watch Vertigo. For a simple yet satisfying story, watch Rear Window .
